page.title: Why People Smell Differently | Simon Cui
hero.title: Why people smell the same odor differently
hero.intro: The same odor can delight one person and repel another. This project uses public human smell ratings to find out where these differences come from, and tries to predict who will like an odor. This is a core question in fragrance development and consumer research.
hero.data: Data: {s} participants rated {m} molecules (each at two concentrations), {n} records in total (Keller & Vosshall, 2016). All results are precomputed.

proc.title: Data processing
proc.intro: Before any analysis, labels are standardized and the data are checked. The rules: different spellings of the same thing are mapped together, problems are flagged and never silently deleted, and every step goes into a processing log.
flow.1.d: {n} rows, one rating of one odor stimulus by one person each
flow.2.d: CAS check digit and a three-way check of CAS, CID and name; {m} molecules mapped to InChIKey, {fix} fixes
flow.3.d: Dilution on a log scale with a high / low label per molecule; {nd} 'cannot smell' rows kept as missing
flow.4.d: Missing, out of range, duplicates; each person's test-retest consistency and scale use; flagged, not removed
flow.5.d: Variance decomposition, personalized prediction, segmentation; exclusion rules compared before and after
proc.issues.title: Identifier problems found and how they were resolved
issue.cas_in_cid.what: A CAS number was typed into the CID column
issue.cas_in_cid.fix: Correct CID looked up in PubChem by CAS or name
issue.cas_bad.what: CAS {cas} fails the check digit, so it is not a valid CAS number
issue.cas_bad.fix: Molecule identified by name; PubChem lists CAS 110-19-0
issue.cid_replaced.what: The sheet's CID points to a different structure (musk ambrette, a nitro musk); name and CAS both point to ambrettolide
issue.cid_replaced.fix: Two against one: CID replaced by the one that name and CAS agree on
issue.manual_keep.what: The CAS number stands for an isomer mixture, which PubChem files under another isomer
issue.manual_keep.fix: Manual decision: the sheet's CID (the structure usually meant by Trivertal) kept, reason logged
issue.unresolved.what: Name not found in PubChem; the CAS points to another ring form
issue.unresolved.fix: Cannot be decided automatically; sheet CID kept. Nearly odorless, negligible effect
issue.name_ambiguous.what: Ambiguous name (for example no isomer given), but CID and CAS agree
proc.issues.note: Four more pairs of molecules become identical without stereo information (for example geraniol and nerol). The graph neural network cannot tell them apart, so each pair is kept in the same fold for the new-molecule test.
proc.retest.title: Is each person consistent?
proc.retest.text: Every participant rated 20 molecules (each at two concentrations) twice. The higher the correlation between the two ratings, the more consistent the person.
proc.retest.sub: One dot per anonymous participant; only stimuli smelled both times (10 to 40 pairs per person)
proc.retest.x: Correlation r between the two ratings
leg.retest_low: Intensity retest r < 0.2 ({n} people, removed in a sensitivity analysis)
proc.retest.note: Individual consistency is only moderate, but the panel average is very stable: split the participants at random into two halves and the average rating of each odor agrees closely between halves (split-half reliability: pleasantness {pr}, intensity {ir}). The noise sits at the level of the individual.
proc.desc.title: Descriptor mapping
proc.desc.text: The 20 descriptors in the data are worded differently from the 138 labels of this site's odor model. A descriptor is mapped only when the meaning is the same AND the data agree (correlation between panel ratings and model predictions ≥ 0.3). The analyses use the original 20 descriptors directly.
desc.not_mapped_same_word_data_disagree: not mapped: same word, data disagree
proc.files: An interesting finding: what lay participants call musky is not the perfumer's musk (the correlation is negative), and fish and sweaty sit closer to sulfurous odors. Consumer language and expert language need to be kept apart. Full mapping tables: molecules, descriptors, concentrations, scales; processing log.
var.title: Where do the differences come from?
var.intro: Each rating is split into parts: the molecule itself, its concentration, the person's general habit (rating everything higher or lower), personal taste (this person's particular reaction to this odor), and measurement noise (the random change between two ratings of the same thing by the same person, estimated from the repeated tests). Only ratings of odors that were smelled are used.
var.sub: All 55 participants, raw scores; hover a segment for its 95% confidence interval
comp.subject: General habit
var.hero.pleasantness: of the reproducible differences in pleasantness come from personal taste (95% CI {lo} to {hi})
var.hero.intensity: of the reproducible differences in intensity come from personal taste (95% CI {lo} to {hi})
var.take: Leaving out noise and rating habits and looking only at the part that belongs to the odor and repeats: people largely agree on how strong an odor is, but whether it is pleasant varies from person to person. Also, about {noise} of a single rating is noise. One rating by one person is not reliable; consumer tests need repeats or more people.
variant.excl_low_retest: Without people with intensity retest r < 0.2
variant.excl_P55: Without P55 only (the least consistent person)
var.method: Method: method of moments. An additive model estimates molecule and person effects; what remains is personal taste plus noise. Noise is estimated separately from the repeated tests and subtracted. On simulated data (known answer, the real missing-data pattern) the estimates are unbiased. Confidence intervals come from a grouped jackknife (leave one person out, plus leave one of 20 molecule blocks out); in simulations the 95% intervals covered the truth in 90% to 100% of runs. Noise can only be estimated from the 20 repeated molecules; their residual variance is close to that of the others (pleasantness {rep} vs {oth}). Noise is not uniform: very strong odors are rated near the top of the scale and vary much less (intensity: strongest third {lo}, middle third {mid}). 'General habit' cannot separate rating style from liking smells in general, so the two are reported together.
spread.title: How big are individual differences?
spread.intro: Pick a molecule and see the pleasantness ratings of everyone who smelled it. People agree on some molecules and are deeply divided on others.
spread.sub: One dot per anonymous participant; {k} of {n} tested participants smelled it
spread.aria: Distribution of individual pleasantness ratings for the selected molecule
spread.note: Standard deviation {sd}: number {rank} by disagreement among the {n} stimuli smelled by at least 45 people (1 = most divisive; median SD {med}).
spread.about.61204: delta-Undecalactone is a common lactone in creamy and dairy aromas.
spread.about.10430: Isovaleric acid is a typical compound of cheesy and sweaty odors.
spread.about.7762: Ethyl butyrate is a common fruity ester.
pred.title: Predicting a new consumer
pred.intro: Suppose a new consumer smells only 5 odors and rates them. Can we predict how much they will like the others? Below is an anonymous participant from the test set (the model never saw this person during training): their 5 known ratings, then the model's predictions for the remaining odors against their actual ratings.
pred.chart.model: Model predictions vs actual ratings ({n} odors)
pred.chart.panel: Panel average vs actual ratings ({n} odors)
pred.chart.sub: Correlation r = {r}, error RMSE = {e}; for comparison, {other}: r = {r2}
pred.aria: Scatter plot of predicted vs actual ratings for a new consumer
pred.rule: The 8 participants are evenly spaced from the lowest to the highest correlation of the model's predictions; they were not picked to look good. The diagonal marks a perfect prediction.
pred.res.title: All results
pred.res.text: Two scenarios, evaluated separately: new molecules (known participants, unseen molecules; 5-fold cross-validation by molecular scaffold) and new consumers (only 5 ratings; 5 folds of participants, 20 random draws). All settings were chosen inside the training part only.
m.global_mean: Overall mean (baseline; a constant, so r is meaningless)
m.reference: Reference: if the panel mean were predicted perfectly
m.probe: Same, with a fixed set of 5 probe odors
pred.curve.title: Do more known ratings help?
pred.curve.sub: New-consumer scenario; number of known ratings on a log scale
pred.take.pleasantness: The model predicts how pleasant an odor is on average fairly well, but beyond a person's overall offset it learns almost nothing about individual preference. For new molecules, the predicted panel mean correlates {pop} with the observed one (the data's own reliability is {rel}); {unseen} for molecules the graph neural network never saw and {seen} for those it did. Personal slopes add only {sl} ({sl0} to {sl1}). Odor-model features are slightly better than structural fingerprints: +{fp} for the population model ({fp0} to {fp1}, includes 0, so not a demonstrated gain). For new consumers, 5 ratings only pin down the overall offset (+{off}, {off0} to {off1}); latent preference factors add almost nothing (+{fac}), and the ranking of odors within a person is the same as with the panel mean alone.
pred.take.intensity: Intensity is easier to predict. For new molecules, the predicted panel mean correlates {pop} with the observed one (the data's own reliability is {rel}); {unseen} for molecules the graph neural network never saw and {seen} for those it did. Odor-model features clearly beat structural fingerprints: +{fp} for the population model ({fp0} to {fp1}). Personal slopes add only {sl} ({sl0} to {sl1}). For new consumers, the gain from 5 ratings comes from the overall offset (+{off}, {off0} to {off1}); latent preference factors add nothing (+{fac}).
seg.title: Consumer segments
seg.intro: Participants are clustered by personal taste, as a stand-in for consumer segmentation. The input is how each person departs from the panel average. The rule was fixed before running: the silhouette must beat the 95th percentile of a no-structure control (each person's ratings shuffled across odors), and clustering two random halves of the molecules must give essentially the same groups (ARI ≥ 0.5).
seg.verdict.no: Conclusion: there are no reliable consumer segments in these data. Individual differences look continuous rather than grouped. Neither clustering method, for k = 2 to 6, with or without the less consistent participants, met the rule: re-cluster on the other half of the molecules and the groups change almost completely. On average, two people's departures from the panel correlate {r}, essentially zero, so the way each person differs from everyone else is mostly their own.
seg.table.note: Hierarchical clustering beats the control on silhouette by a little, but its stability ARI is close to 0: the groups are made by noise and do not repeat. k-means often splits off groups of one.
seg.axis.title: The one reproducible dimension
seg.axis.text: With no clear groups, the next question is whether individual differences share a direction. The first principal direction explains only {v} of individual differences (no-structure control {vn}), but it repeats: computed on two different halves of the molecules, people's scores correlate {r} (control {rn}). It mainly reflects tolerance of strong odors: the direction correlates {ri} with odor intensity.
seg.scores.title: Where the 55 participants sit on this dimension
seg.scores.sub: One dot per anonymous participant; the spread is continuous, with no visible clumps
seg.desc.title: With intensity removed, which descriptors go with this dimension?
seg.desc.sub: Partial correlation between each descriptor's panel rating and the dimension, with odor intensity partialled out
seg.axis.note: People's scores on this dimension are essentially unrelated to quality measures (share of odors not smelled, rating habits, test-retest consistency; |ρ| ≤ {q}), so it is not an artefact of data quality. The second direction explains {v2} with reproducibility {r2} (control {rn2}), barely above the control, so it is not interpreted.
res.title: Results and limitations
res.1: Pleasantness is mainly a matter of personal taste: about six tenths of its reproducible differences are personal. Intensity is mainly decided by the molecule and its concentration. This holds under every exclusion rule and processing choice tried.
res.2: The model predicts panel-average ratings reasonably well, and the graph neural network's odor features beat structural fingerprints (clearly so for intensity). Beyond an overall offset, individual preference can hardly be learned from a few ratings.
res.3: There are no reliable consumer segments. Individual differences are continuous; the only reproducible direction mainly reflects tolerance of strong odors.
res.4: For consumer research: single ratings are very noisy, so tests need repeats. Getting the population prediction right and then adjusting along dimensions that can be verified is safer than assuming fixed consumer groups.
lim.title: Limitations
lim.1: The data come from single molecules rated in a laboratory, not real products and not real consumption situations.
lim.2: Only 55 participants, all from the New York area, so group-level conclusions have limited reach; finding no segments here does not mean a real market has none.
lim.3: Only explicit ratings; no implicit data such as neural or physiological measures.
lim.4: The descriptor mapping involves human judgement, which is why the analyses use the original 20 descriptors.
lim.5: Noise can only be estimated from 20 repeated molecules and changes with the rating level; the variance decomposition assumes it generalizes to all stimuli.
lim.6: The graph neural network saw the odor labels of 388 molecules of these data during its training, so predictions for them are optimistic; results for unseen molecules are reported separately.
eth.title: Data ethics
eth.1: The original study was approved by The Rockefeller University Institutional Review Board (protocol LVO-0780), participants gave written informed consent, and the authors released the data under CC0.
eth.2: Demographics (gender, age, race, ethnicity) were dropped at import. No analysis or conclusion is based on demographic information.
eth.3: Participants were recoded at random as P01 to P55; the codes on this page cannot be linked to personal information in the original public sheet. Participants' own free-text descriptions are not used or shown.
eth.4: The raw data are not uploaded to this site's repository; the page publishes summaries and anonymous rating values only.
footer.data: Data: Keller A, Vosshall LB. Olfactory perception of chemically diverse molecules. BMC Neuroscience 2016; 17: 55. doi:10.1186/s12868-016-0287-2. Article CC BY 4.0, data CC0. The data were also used in the DREAM Olfaction Prediction Challenge.
